name: Earth and Space Science
author: Recurse
subject: science
description: Plate tectonics, rocks and deep time, climate and the greenhouse effect, seasons, the Moon, stars and the scale of space.

lesson.intro: Earth is a restless planet: its surface moves, its rocks are recycled, and its air and oceans carry the Sun's heat around the globe. This lesson covers how Earth works, why we have seasons and Moon phases, and where Earth sits in a universe far larger than intuition suggests.
objectives: Describe Earth's layers and explain what happens at each type of plate boundary
Classify rocks by how they formed, and date them with superposition and half-lives
Distinguish weather from climate and explain how the greenhouse effect works
Explain seasons, Moon phases and eclipses with the right geometry
Describe how stars shine and die, and use AU and light-years to grasp the scale of space

sections.title: Earth's layers and plate tectonics
sections.body:
Earth is built in layers, densest at the center:

- Crust: the thin, rocky outer skin. It is about 5 to 10 km thick under the oceans and 30 to 50 km thick under the continents, more under big mountain ranges.
- Mantle: hot rock down to a depth of about 2,900 km. It is almost entirely solid, but over millions of years it flows very slowly, like extremely stiff putty.
- Outer core: liquid iron and nickel, from about 2,900 to 5,150 km down. Its churning generates Earth's magnetic field.
- Inner core: a solid ball of iron and nickel, from about 5,150 km down to the center at 6,371 km. It is roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun but stays solid because of the enormous pressure.

The crust and the rigid top of the mantle form the lithosphere, which is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. The plates move a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow, driven by heat escaping from Earth's interior and by the pull of plate edges sinking into the mantle. Where plates meet, they interact in three ways:

- Divergent boundaries: plates pull apart, and magma rises to fill the gap and form new crust, as along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
- Convergent boundaries: plates push together. A dense oceanic plate sinks beneath the other plate (subduction), forming a deep trench and a line of volcanoes, as in the Andes and Japan. Where two continents collide, neither sinks easily, and the crust crumples into mountains such as the Himalayas.
- Transform boundaries: plates slide sideways past each other, causing earthquakes, as along California's San Andreas Fault.

That is why most earthquakes and volcanoes occur in narrow bands along plate edges, such as the Ring of Fire around the Pacific Ocean.
sections.code:
Layer         Depth (km)        State
Crust         0 to 5–50         solid rock
Mantle        to ~2,900         solid, flows very slowly
Outer core    ~2,900 to 5,150   liquid iron and nickel
Inner core    ~5,150 to 6,371   solid iron and nickel
sections.tip: The mantle is not an ocean of magma. Molten rock forms only in limited places, such as under mid-ocean ridges, above sinking plates and at hotspots like Hawaii.
sections.pitfall: Picturing the mantle as an ocean of magma. It is solid rock that flows extremely slowly; the only liquid layer is the outer core.

check.question: The Himalayas are still rising. What kind of plate boundary formed them?
choices: Divergent: two plates pulling apart
Convergent: two continental plates colliding
Transform: two plates sliding past each other
A hotspot in the middle of a plate
check.explanation: The Indian plate is pushing into the Eurasian plate. Neither continent sinks easily, so the crust crumples and thickens into the world's highest mountains, which are still rising by a few millimeters a year.

sections.title: The rock cycle
sections.body:
Geologists sort rocks into three types by how they formed.

- Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and hardens. Magma that cools slowly underground grows large crystals, as in granite. Lava that cools quickly at the surface makes tiny crystals, as in basalt, or even natural glass, as in obsidian.
- Sedimentary rocks form when weathering and erosion break rock into fragments (sediment), which settle in layers, get buried, and are compacted and cemented together. Sandstone, shale and limestone are examples. Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock, because buried remains are preserved without being melted or crushed.
- Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting. Limestone becomes marble, shale becomes slate, and granite can become gneiss.

These types are linked in a cycle. Any rock can be weathered into sediment, buried and transformed by heat and pressure, or melted and cooled again. Earth's internal heat drives melting, metamorphism and the uplift of mountains, while sunlight drives the weather and flowing water that wear rocks down. One trip around the cycle usually takes millions of years.

In undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, older layers lie below younger ones. This principle, called superposition, lets geologists read rock layers like the pages of a history book.
sections.code:
any rock     → weathering and erosion → sediment → sedimentary rock
any rock     → heat and pressure, no melting     → metamorphic rock
any rock     → melting → magma → cooling         → igneous rock
sections.tip: Ask how a rock formed: from melt (igneous), from settled particles (sedimentary), or from changed rock (metamorphic).
sections.pitfall: Thinking a rock's type is permanent. Given enough time, weathering, heat, pressure or melting can turn any rock type into any other.

check.question: Marble forms when limestone is heated and squeezed deep underground without melting. What type of rock is marble?
choices: Igneous
Sedimentary
Metamorphic
Volcanic
check.explanation: Marble is limestone transformed by heat and pressure without melting, which is exactly what makes a rock metamorphic. If the limestone had melted and then cooled, the result would be an igneous rock instead.

sections.title: Deep time: dating rocks and Earth's history
sections.body:
A road cut through a hillside shows stripes of rock stacked like a layer cake. Reading those stripes, and the atoms inside them, is how geologists worked out that Earth is about 4.54 billion years old.

**Relative dating** puts events in order without numbers. By superposition, lower layers in undisturbed rock are older. By cross-cutting, anything that slices across layers, such as a fault or a vein of igneous rock that forced its way up as magma, is younger than the layers it cuts. Fossils help match layers between distant places, because particular species lived only during particular spans of time.

**Absolute dating** attaches numbers, using radioactive isotopes as clocks. A radioactive isotope decays at a fixed rate measured by its **half-life**, the time for half its atoms to decay. After one half-life, 1/2 of the original amount remains; after two, 1/4; after three, 1/8. Measure how much of the parent isotope is left compared with what it turns into, and you can count the half-lives that have passed.

Different clocks suit different ages. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years, so it dates once-living things up to about 50,000 years old: a bone with 1/4 of its original carbon-14 is about 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years old. Old rocks need slower clocks such as uranium-238, whose half-life is about 4.5 billion years.

The resulting timeline is hard to picture. Squeeze Earth's whole history into one calendar year, starting January 1. The first animals with shells and skeletons appear around mid-November, the dinosaurs die out on December 26 (66 million years ago, after an asteroid impact), and modern humans show up at about 11:25 pm on December 31.
sections.code:
Half-lives passed    Fraction of parent left
0                    1
1                    1/2
2                    1/4
3                    1/8
4                    1/16

Earth forms                        4.54 billion years ago
First evidence of life             about 3.5 billion years ago
Oxygen builds up in the air        about 2.4 billion years ago
Cambrian explosion of animals      about 539 million years ago
Dinosaurs (except birds) die out   66 million years ago
Modern humans                      about 300,000 years ago
sections.pitfall: Assuming carbon-14 dates rocks or dinosaurs. With a 5,730-year half-life, too little is left after about 50,000 years; old rocks are dated with slow clocks such as uranium-lead.

check.question: A bone has 1/8 of its original carbon-14 left. Carbon-14's half-life is 5,730 years. About how old is the bone?
choices: 5,730 years
11,460 years
17,190 years
45,840 years
check.explanation: 1/8 is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2, so three half-lives have passed: 3 × 5,730 = 17,190 years. 45,840 years multiplies by 8, treating the decay as linear instead of halving.

sections.title: Water, weather, climate and the greenhouse effect
sections.body:
The water cycle moves water between the oceans, the air and the land, powered by energy from the Sun and by gravity.

- Evaporation: sunlight warms oceans, lakes and soil, and liquid water turns to vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves (transpiration). The salt stays behind, which is why rain is fresh even though the oceans, which hold about 97% of Earth's water, are salty.
- Condensation: rising air cools, and the vapor condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds.
- Precipitation: droplets merge until they are heavy enough to fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
- Collection: water runs off into rivers and back to the sea, or soaks into the ground to become groundwater.

Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a given place and time: today's temperature, wind, clouds and rain. Climate is the average pattern of weather in a region over a long period, usually 30 years or more. Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get. One cold week says little about the climate, just as one hot day does not prove warming on its own.

The greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. Sunlight, mostly visible light, passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface. The warm surface gives off infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases such as water vapor, carbon dioxide (CO₂) and methane absorb much of that infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the ground. Without this effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C.

Burning fossil fuels has raised the CO₂ in the air from about 280 parts per million (ppm) before the Industrial Revolution to more than 420 ppm today. Human greenhouse gas emissions, mostly this extra CO₂, are the main cause of the global warming measured since the late 1800s. The ozone hole is a different problem: the ozone layer blocks ultraviolet light, and its thinning is not what drives global warming.
sections.code:
Sunlight (visible) passes through the air  →  surface warms
Warm surface gives off infrared            →  greenhouse gases absorb it
Gases re-emit infrared, some back down     →  surface stays warmer

With no greenhouse effect:  about −18 °C average
Actual average:             about 15 °C
sections.tip: Weather is measured in hours and days; climate is measured in decades of averages.
sections.pitfall: Judging the climate from one season or one storm. Climate is a 30-year average; a cold week or a hot day is weather.

check.question: Which statement describes climate rather than weather?
choices: It is snowing in the mountains right now
This region averages about 50 cm of rain a year, mostly in winter
Tomorrow will be windy along the coast
A thunderstorm passed through town last night
check.explanation: A long-term average for a region describes its climate. The other three statements describe conditions at one particular time, which is weather.

sections.title: Seasons, Moon phases and eclipses
sections.body:
Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4° relative to its orbit, and the axis keeps pointing the same way in space as Earth travels around the Sun. For part of the year the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun. There, the Sun climbs higher in the sky, so its light strikes the ground more directly and concentrates more energy on each square meter, and the days are longer. That is summer. Six months later the Northern Hemisphere leans away from the Sun, and it is winter.

Seasons are not caused by changes in distance. Earth's orbit is nearly a circle, and Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter. The clearest evidence is that the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time, which a change in distance could never explain.

The Moon shines by reflected sunlight, and the Sun always lights one half of it. As the Moon orbits Earth, taking about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next, we see different amounts of that lit half:

- New moon: the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, and its lit side faces away from us.
- Waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous: the lit part we can see grows.
- Full moon: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and we see the whole lit half.
- Waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent: the lit part shrinks back toward new moon.

Earth's shadow plays no part in the phases. It falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.

- A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, so the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. It can only happen at new moon.
- A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can only happen at full moon.

Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's orbit. In most months, the Moon passes a little above or below the line joining Earth and the Sun.

Four dates mark the year. At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere leans most toward the Sun: it has its longest day, the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest, and the noon Sun stands directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer (23.4° N). The December solstice is the mirror image. At the March and September equinoxes neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and day and night are roughly equal everywhere.
sections.code:
Axis tilt:                    about 23.4°
Closest to Sun (perihelion):  early January, about 147 million km
Farthest (aphelion):          early July, about 152 million km

Solar eclipse:   Sun – Moon – Earth    (new moon only)
Lunar eclipse:   Sun – Earth – Moon    (full moon only)
sections.tip: If seasons came from distance, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time. Instead they have opposite seasons.
sections.pitfall: Explaining the seasons by distance from the Sun. Earth is closest in January, and the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same moment.

check.question: At full moon, where is the Moon compared with Earth and the Sun?
choices: On the far side of Earth from the Sun
Between Earth and the Sun
Directly above Earth's North Pole
At a right angle to the line from Earth to the Sun
check.explanation: At full moon, Earth lies roughly between the Sun and the Moon, so the side of the Moon facing us is fully lit. Between Earth and the Sun is the new moon position, and a right angle gives the quarter phases.

sections.title: The solar system and the scale of the universe
sections.body:
The solar system is the Sun and everything held in orbit around it by gravity. The Sun contains about 99.8% of the solar system's mass. Eight planets orbit it:

- Four small rocky planets close to the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
- Two gas giants: Jupiter, the largest planet, and Saturn.
- Two ice giants: Uranus and Neptune.

Beyond Neptune lie dwarf planets such as Pluto, which was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and countless smaller icy bodies. Distance from the Sun is not the only thing that sets a planet's temperature. Venus, second from the Sun, is hotter than Mercury, at about 465 °C on the surface, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect.

Distances in space are so large that kilometers become clumsy:

- The astronomical unit (AU) is the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross it.
- A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km. Despite its name, it is a distance, not a time.

Light travels about 300,000 km every second. Even so, light from the nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, takes about 4.2 years to reach us. Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is about 100,000 light-years across and holds hundreds of billions of stars. It is just one of hundreds of billions of galaxies in the observable universe.

Because light takes time to travel, looking farther away means looking back in time. We see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago, and the Andromeda Galaxy as it was about 2.5 million years ago.
sections.code:
1 AU          ≈ 150 million km     (light takes ~8 min 20 s)
1 light-year  ≈ 9.46 trillion km
Proxima Centauri, nearest star after the Sun: ~4.2 light-years
Milky Way: ~100,000 light-years across

1 light-year = 299,792 km/s × 31,557,600 s ≈ 9.46 × 10¹² km
sections.tip: A light-year sounds like a time but measures distance, the way "a ten-minute walk" can tell you how far away a shop is.
sections.pitfall: Treating a light-year as a length of time. It is a distance, about 9.46 trillion km, even though it is defined using a year.

check.question: Which planet has the hottest surface, and why?
choices: Mercury, because it is closest to the Sun
Jupiter, because it is the largest planet
Mars, because its red soil absorbs sunlight
Venus, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat
check.explanation: Venus's dense CO₂ atmosphere creates a runaway greenhouse effect that keeps its surface at about 465 °C, day and night. Mercury is closer to the Sun, but with almost no atmosphere it cannot hold on to heat, and its night side becomes extremely cold.

sections.title: Stars: how they shine and how they end
sections.body:
The Sun has been shining steadily for about 4.6 billion years without burning up. It is not a fire: its power comes from **nuclear fusion** in its core, where a temperature of about 15 million °C forces hydrogen nuclei together to make helium. Every second, the Sun turns about 4 million metric tons of its mass into energy, following E = mc².

A star is a balancing act. Gravity pulls all its gas inward, and the pressure of the hot gas pushes outward. While fusion supplies energy the two stay balanced, and the star spends most of its life in this steady stage, called the main sequence.

A star's color tells its surface temperature. Red stars are the coolest, at about 3,000 °C; yellow stars like the Sun are about 5,500 °C; blue-white stars are the hottest, above 10,000 °C.

Mass decides how a star lives and dies:

- Stars like the Sun live about 10 billion years. When the hydrogen in the core runs low, the star swells into a **red giant**, later puffs off its outer layers, and leaves behind a **white dwarf**: a hot core about the size of Earth that slowly cools. The Sun has about 5 billion years of core hydrogen left.
- Massive stars, more than about 8 times the Sun's mass, burn hot and fast and live only millions of years. They end in a **supernova** explosion. The collapsed core becomes a **neutron star**, a city-sized ball so dense that a teaspoon would weigh about a billion tons, or, for the heaviest stars, a **black hole**, whose gravity is so strong that not even light escapes.

Almost every element heavier than helium was made in stars. Fusion in massive stars builds elements up to iron, and heavier elements such as gold form in supernovae and in collisions between neutron stars. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were forged in stars that died before the Sun was born.
sections.code:
Mass (Sun = 1)   Main-sequence life                     End
0.5              longer than the universe's age so far   white dwarf
1 (the Sun)      about 10 billion years                  red giant, then white dwarf
20               about 10 million years                  supernova, then neutron star or black hole
sections.pitfall: Thinking the Sun will explode as a supernova. It is far too light: it will swell into a red giant and end as a white dwarf.

check.question: What powers the Sun?
choices: Hydrogen burning with oxygen, like a fire
Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core
Nuclear fission of uranium
Gravity slowly squeezing it smaller
check.explanation: The Sun's core fuses hydrogen into helium, converting a little mass into a lot of energy. Chemical burning would have used up a Sun-sized fuel supply in a few thousand years, and fission powers nuclear reactors, not stars.

keyTerms.definition: A large slab of Earth's lithosphere that moves slowly over the mantle.
The sinking of a dense oceanic plate beneath another plate at a convergent boundary.
Rock changed by heat and pressure without melting, such as marble or slate.
The long-term average pattern of weather in a region, usually measured over 30 years or more.
The warming of a planet's surface when gases in its atmosphere absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit some of it back down.
The roughly 23.4° tilt of Earth's axis, which causes the seasons.
Earth's shadow falling on the Moon when Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon; possible only at full moon.
The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km.
The time it takes for half of a radioactive isotope's atoms to decay; the basis of radiometric dating.
Light nuclei joining to form a heavier one and releasing energy; in the Sun's core, hydrogen fuses into helium.
The explosion of a massive star at the end of its life, leaving a neutron star or a black hole.

summary: Earth has a thin crust, a solid but slowly flowing mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core; moving plates cause earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.
Rocks form from melt, sediment or heat and pressure; superposition and radioactive half-lives date them and show Earth is about 4.54 billion years old.
Weather is short-term conditions and climate is the long-term average; greenhouse gases keep Earth warm, and extra CO₂ is warming it further.
Seasons come from axial tilt, not distance; Moon phases come from our viewing angle, and eclipses need an exact Sun–Earth–Moon line-up.
Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium, and a star's mass decides whether it ends as a white dwarf or in a supernova.
A light-year is a distance, and looking deep into space means seeing light that left its source long ago.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why it is summer in Australia when it is winter in Canada, and why the Moon looks like a crescent on some nights even though Earth's shadow is nowhere near it.

questions.question: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
choices: The mantle
The outer core
The inner core
The crust
questions.explanation: The outer core is molten iron and nickel, and its flow generates Earth's magnetic field. The mantle is often pictured as liquid magma, but it is almost entirely solid rock that flows only very slowly. The inner core is even hotter than the outer core but stays solid under enormous pressure.

questions.question: New Zealand's Alpine Fault is where the Pacific and Australian plates mainly grind sideways past each other. What type of plate boundary is this?
choices: Divergent
Convergent
Transform
Subduction zone
questions.explanation: Plates sliding horizontally past each other form a transform boundary, where stress builds up and is released in earthquakes. New crust forms at divergent boundaries, and crust sinks at subduction zones, which are a kind of convergent boundary.

questions.question: Describe what happens at divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries.
questions.answer: At divergent boundaries, plates move apart and rising magma forms new crust. At convergent boundaries, plates collide: one may sink beneath the other, forming trenches and volcanoes, or two continents crumple into mountains. At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes.
questions.explanation: Examples: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is divergent, the Andes and the Himalayas formed at convergent boundaries, and the San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary.

questions.question: Which type of rock is most likely to contain fossils?
choices: Sedimentary
Igneous
Metamorphic
Volcanic glass
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rock forms from layers of sediment that bury remains gently and at low temperature, so they can be preserved. Igneous rock forms from melted rock, which destroys remains, and the heat and pressure that make metamorphic rock usually distort or erase any fossils.

questions.question: Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks, but granite has large, visible crystals while basalt's are tiny. Why?
choices: Granite is older, so its crystals have had longer to grow
Basalt was crushed by pressure, which broke up its crystals
Granite formed from sediment, while basalt formed from lava
Granite cooled slowly underground; basalt cooled quickly at the surface
questions.explanation: Crystal size depends on how fast molten rock cools. Magma that cools slowly deep underground gives crystals time to grow large, while lava that cools quickly at the surface hardens before crystals can grow. Crystals do not keep growing once a rock is solid, so age is not the reason.

questions.question: What type of rock forms when magma or lava cools and hardens?
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form from molten rock. Sedimentary rocks form from compacted sediment, and metamorphic rocks form from existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting.

questions.question: A city has its coldest week in decades. What does this tell you about global climate change?
choices: That global warming has stopped
That this region's climate is now cooling
Very little: one week is weather, and climate is a long-term average
That scientists have been measuring the climate wrongly
questions.explanation: Climate describes averages over 30 years or more. A single cold week is weather, and cold snaps still happen in a warming climate; they just become less common on average. Judging the climate from one week is like judging a season from one day.

questions.question: Ocean water is salty, yet rain is fresh water. Why?
choices: Clouds filter the salt out of the vapor
Salt is left behind when water evaporates
Salt falls back out of clouds as snow
Rain comes only from evaporated lake water
questions.explanation: Only water molecules evaporate; the dissolved salt stays in the ocean. The vapor that later condenses and falls as rain is therefore fresh. Clouds do not filter anything, because the salt never left the sea in the first place.

questions.question: How do greenhouse gases warm Earth's surface?
choices: They block sunlight from reaching the ground
They produce heat through chemical reactions in the air
They thin the ozone layer, letting in more sunlight
They absorb infrared given off by the surface and re-emit some back down
questions.explanation: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground, which then radiates infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb that infrared and send part of it back, so the surface stays warmer than it otherwise would. Ozone loss is a separate problem involving ultraviolet light, not the cause of the greenhouse effect.

questions.question: Which greenhouse gas has risen from about 280 ppm to more than 420 ppm since the Industrial Revolution, mainly from burning fossil fuels? Give its name or formula.
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, CO₂. Methane is rising too, but it is measured in parts per billion, not hundreds of parts per million. Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but its amount follows temperature rather than being set directly by emissions.

questions.question: What is the main cause of Earth's seasons?
choices: The tilt of Earth's axis changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere
Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
The Sun gives off more energy in summer
Earth spins faster in summer
questions.explanation: The tilted axis means each hemisphere spends part of the year leaning toward the Sun, with the Sun higher in the sky and longer days. Distance cannot be the cause: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, during northern winter, and the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.

questions.question: In which month is Earth closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Earth reaches perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in early January, at about 147 million km, which is during the Northern Hemisphere's winter. That alone shows distance does not cause the seasons.

questions.question: During which phase of the Moon can a solar eclipse happen?
choices: Full moon
New moon
First quarter
Any phase
questions.explanation: A solar eclipse needs the Moon directly between the Sun and Earth, which is where it is at new moon. Full moon is the phase for a lunar eclipse, when Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon.

questions.question: What causes the phases of the Moon?
choices: Earth's shadow covering part of the Moon
Clouds hiding part of the Moon from view
Seeing different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth
The Moon's own light dimming and brightening
questions.explanation: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits, we see that lit half from different angles, from none of it at new moon to all of it at full moon. Earth's shadow reaches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which happens at full moon and looks quite different from a phase.

questions.question: What does a light-year measure?
choices: Distance
Time
Speed
Brightness
questions.explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km. Despite the word year, it is a unit of length, used because the distances between stars are far too large for kilometers to be practical.

questions.question: To the nearest minute, how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.explanation: Earth is about 150 million km from the Sun, and light covers about 300,000 km each second: 150,000,000 / 300,000 = 500 seconds, a little over 8 minutes. So we always see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago.
questions.concept: speed of light and the AU

questions.question: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away. Why does looking at it mean looking into the past?
questions.answer: Its light has been traveling for about 2.5 million years to reach us, so we see Andromeda as it was when that light set out, not as it is today.
questions.explanation: The same is true of everything we see: the Moon as it was about 1.3 seconds ago, the Sun about 8 minutes ago. The farther away an object is, the older the light we receive from it.

questions.question: Match each rock to how it formed.

pairs.right: Igneous: lava cooled quickly at the surface
Metamorphic: limestone changed by heat and pressure
Metamorphic: shale changed by heat and pressure

questions.explanation: Igneous rocks come from melt, and their crystal size records the cooling speed. Sedimentary rocks are compacted, cemented sediment. Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks changed without melting: limestone to marble, shale to slate.

questions.question: Starting from new moon, put the Moon's phases in order.
questions.explanation: Waxing means the visible lit part is growing, toward full moon; waning means it is shrinking, back toward new moon. The whole cycle takes about 29.5 days.

questions.question: Put these events in Earth's history in order, oldest first.
items: Oxygen builds up in the atmosphere
Animals with shells and skeletons spread in the Cambrian
questions.explanation: Earth formed 4.54 billion years ago, life appeared by about 3.5 billion, oxygen built up about 2.4 billion years ago, the Cambrian began about 539 million years ago, the dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago, and modern humans appeared about 300,000 years ago.

questions.question: A rock has 25% of its original uranium-235 left. The half-life of U-235 is about 704 million years. About how old is the rock, in millions of years?
questions.explanation: 25% is 1/2 × 1/2, so two half-lives have passed: 2 × 704 = 1,408 million years, about 1.4 billion. Dividing 704 by 4 or multiplying by 4 treats decay as a straight line rather than repeated halving.

questions.question: Which statement is true at the June solstice?
choices: Earth is at its closest to the Sun
Day and night are equal everywhere
The Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day of the year
The noon Sun is directly overhead at the equator
questions.explanation: In June the Northern Hemisphere leans most toward the Sun, so the south has its shortest day and the noon Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Earth is actually near its farthest point from the Sun then, and equal day and night belongs to the equinoxes.

questions.question: Select every statement that is true of the Sun.
choices: It is powered by fusing hydrogen into helium
It will end its life as a supernova
It will swell into a red giant
Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth
It holds about half of the solar system's mass
questions.explanation: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, will become a red giant and then a white dwarf, and its light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach us. It is too light to go supernova, and it holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass, not half.

questions.question: Which star has the hottest surface?
choices: A red star
An orange star
A yellow star like the Sun
A blue-white star
questions.explanation: Star color tracks surface temperature: red is coolest (about 3,000 °C), yellow is in the middle (the Sun is about 5,500 °C), and blue-white is hottest. It is the opposite of the everyday habit of calling red hot and blue cold.

questions.question: About how old is Earth, in billions of years?
questions.explanation: Radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest Earth minerals gives about 4.54 billion years. The Sun and the rest of the solar system formed at about the same time.

questions.question: In an undisturbed cliff, layer A lies on top of layer B, and a band of igneous rock cuts straight through both layers. What is the order of events, oldest first?
choices: A, then B, then the igneous band
The igneous band, then B, then A
B, then the igneous band, then A
B, then A, then the igneous band
questions.explanation: By superposition, the lower layer B is older than A. By cross-cutting, the igneous band must be younger than every layer it cuts, so it came last. If it had formed before A, it would stop at A's base instead of cutting through.

questions.question: What is the most likely fate of a star with 20 times the Sun's mass?
choices: It cools quietly into a white dwarf
It explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole
It shrinks until it becomes a planet
It shines steadily for hundreds of billions of years
questions.explanation: Stars above about 8 solar masses burn through their fuel in millions of years and end in a supernova, leaving a neutron star or, for the heaviest, a black hole. White dwarfs are the end of Sun-like stars, and long lives belong to small, cool stars.

questions.question: A friend says global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer letting more heat in. What is the best correction?
choices: That is right: the ozone hole is the main cause of warming
Warming happens because Earth is moving closer to the Sun
Ozone loss lets in more ultraviolet; warming comes mainly from greenhouse gases trapping outgoing infrared
Warming comes from volcanoes, not from human activity
questions.explanation: The ozone layer blocks ultraviolet light, a separate problem. The warming measured since the late 1800s comes mainly from extra greenhouse gases, chiefly CO₂ from fossil fuels, absorbing infrared from the surface. Volcanoes emit far less CO₂ than human activity.

questions.question: Why is there not a solar eclipse at every new moon?
choices: The Moon is too small to cover the Sun
Earth's shadow gets in the way at new moon
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so it usually passes above or below the Sun
Most months the eclipse happens at night for everyone
questions.explanation: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's orbit, so at most new moons its shadow misses Earth. When a new moon happens near the line where the two orbits cross, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and an eclipse occurs somewhere on Earth.
